speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: WEST INDIES FEDERATION-STATEMENT ON PRESENTATION OF CLERKS' TABLES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it will be recalled that at the time of the inauguration ceremonies of the federal legislature of the West Indies in 1958, the ministers representing the government and people of Canada stated that a presentation of two clerks' tables would be made by Canada to the federation, one for the house of representatives and the other for the senate, to commemorate the occasion. These presentations will be made this afternoon by the commissioner for Canada, Mr. R. G. C. Smith.
This house, too, bears evidence on every hand of similar presentations. No doubt most hon. members are aware that your chair, sir, was presented to the parliament of Canada in 1921 by the United Kingdom branch of the empire parliamentary association. Incorporated into it were portions of the old oak roof of Westminster hall which was constructed in 1397. The mace was, of course, a gift from the United Kingdom, presented by the lord mayor and sheriffs of London in 1916. So, in taking the course we do, we but follow an example which has been set on previous occasions.
The gifts which are being presented to the West Indies legislature, like the gifts which repose in this house, serve as tangible reminders of the continuity and the growth in strength of parliamentary government and of the close and cordial relations which exist between the various parts of the commonwealth. I am sure hon. members in all parts of the house will wish to join with me on this occasion in extending our very best wishes to the federation of the West Indies.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
subtopic: WEST INDIES FEDERATION-STATEMENT ON PRESENTATION OF CLERKS' TABLES
speechtext:
We on this side of the house have heard with great pleasure and approval the statement the Prime Minister has just
made, and we agree that the presentation of clerks' tables to the parliament of the new federation will be a reminder that both federations have inherited the same parliamentary traditions. It will also be an indication of the good will of the parliament and people of this country to the new federation as it enters on the first stage of its constitutional existence, and the desire of the people of Canada to maintain the closest and friendliest relations with this other western hemisphere nation of the commonwealth.

subtopic: WEST INDIES FEDERATION-STATEMENT ON PRESENTATION OF CLERKS' TABLES
speechtext:
On
behalf of this group, Mr. Speaker, I wish to say that we consider this a most appropriate gift to this new member of the commonwealth. It stands as a symbol of our common parliamentary heritage, traditions and procedures, and is a visible indication of our good will and best wishes for their every success in the future.

Mr. Speaker, I find that in the bill ;here is no departure from the language ised or from the announcements made at arovious stages of the debate, on budget night and when the resolution was being discussed.
Excise Act
I simply wish to remind the house that we are being asked here to provide an all-time high rate of taxation on distilled spirits.
I believe that prior to the introduction of this bill the excise tax amounted to $1.31 on a 25-ounce bottle of distilled spirits. The increase will bring this figure to $1.42, with sales tax to be paid in addition. As in so many other cases connected with this budget, we find there has been a desire on the part of those who merchandise a product to do some profiteering beyond what the increase resulting from taxation would have justified. Even my own province of Ontario was not slow in this respect. The authorities immediately imposed an increase in price well beyond the amount which the Minister of Finance had announced would be the net tax cost increase per 25-ounce bottle of spirits.
We know that as a result of criticism the government of Ontario did decide to lower those prices. It may have had something to do with the subsequent decision to hold an election. I do not know. Perhaps it was the result of a comment by the Prime Minister, who said that merchandisers were improperly and unjustifiably raising prices to consumers beyond the additional amount of taxation. In any event, we have seen that the liquor control board in Ontario, and perhaps in other provinces too where there is a government monopoly, has since reduced the price to the consumer to a figure which more nearly takes account only of the extra amount of the tax.
I have heard the Minister of Finance speak in the past about taxation in fields of this kind, and he always used to warn his predecessors that there was a point of diminishing return. I hope the minister, who never wants to appear wrong in front of the public, may never have to do what his colleague the Minister of National Revenue suggested he might have to do, and play some personal part in trying to make up the deficiency in tax revenue if there are diminishing returns.
In any event, we have in connection with this product an all-time high rate of government taxation either in peacetime or wartime.

Looking at the proposed amendments to the Excise Tax Act, Mr. Speaker, it is very obvious that the Minister of Finance is against evil. We have often had ministers of finance who where against evil, and when they needed more revenue they simply levied taxes on the people of Canada who consume liquor or who have the habit of smoking.
I feel that a growing number of people in Canada are becoming increasingly irritated

Excise Act
about this attitude which various ministers of finance have taken over the years. They feel that there is a limit beyond which their particular weakness or vice if you want to call it that should not be exploited. I am saying this merely for the sake of the readers of Hansard, that a bottle of ordinary liquor, rye for example, could be purchased for roughly $1.10 if it were not subject to taxation. Yet, after the various levels of government have taken their toll, the Canadian consumer finds he has to pay around $3.00 extra. A package of 20 Canadian cigarettes can be purchased, in those places where it is tax exempt, for 9 cents. Yet, in Ontario today people are asked to pay 35 cents a package.
I do not like this continued punishment of what some puritanically-minded people may consider to be a vice. I believe it is high time that the majority of the people of Canada began to voice their opinions about these continued impositions year after year upon practices which they regard as unharmful but which a minority regard as harmful. However, it seems that the days are few and far between when public representatives are willing to make their voices heard on behalf of those people who occasionally buy a bottle of whisky or a package of smokes. I feel that if there is a need for added taxation in Canada we should not take it out on these people simply because there are no members of parliament ready to take up the case on their behalf.

speakeroldname: Hon. Donald M. Fleming (Minister ot Finance) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: the second reading of Bill No. C-46, to amend the Old Age Security Act.

Mr. Speaker, I made some remarks with respect to these three tax increases at the resolution stage on May 4, appearing at page 3306 of Hansard, and I believe some amplification of those remarks is justified.
The Minister of Finance and I had the privilege of serving together, I believe in 1950, on the joint parliamentary committee which looked at the question of ways and means of improving social security for the aged, and I think he will agree with me that that committee was a most useful one. It also was quite devoid of partisanship in the preparation of its report.
It is true that the committee did not lay down in a dogmatic way recommendations to the government as to how the improved social legislation should be financed. I am not going to read the committee's recommendations, but they are contained at page 703 of the committee report of June 28, 1950.
The committee agreed that it was desirable to have basically a pay as you go system for supporting old age security. It did not specifically instruct the government as to how this might be financed. It did point out the fact that certain important tax sources might on a percentage basis provide the necessary revenues. On the whole I believe the committee was recommending a compromise between what would be called contributory old age pension system, on the insurance pattern such as we examined in respect of other countries, and the matter of having the fund in balance at all times.
The committee at no time said the fund should be completely in balance. It recognized that in the past the federal treasury had been responsible for making contributions out of general revenues to certain social security measures existing up to that time and, as I said, did not dogmatically state that the fund should be completely in balance. In other words there was the thought that if there was an occasional deficit in connection with the fund it might be reconciled with the amount of revenue that had been utilized previously from general taxation in the past.
However, the following year the government did decide that it would apply to three of the important tax fields for contributions to the very widely expanded old age security plan that was introduced in 1951. It introduced what was known as the 2-2-2 formula. The minister is proposing in this legislation a 50 per cent increase in that form of tax receipt.
In 1952 the revenues that were received were not actually to be new taxes in the main. That is the difference between what
Old Age Security Act
the minister is proposing now and what the government of that day proposed when this legislation was introduced in 1951. It may be said that with a very slight exception instead of increasing existing taxes the new fund was provided with allocated revenues, but it did not involve extra taxes for that purpose affecting the actual individual taxpayer of the country. The existing tax rate was adjusted in such a way that there was assigned without increase in rates 2 per cent of the sales tax, 2 per cent of the corporation tax and 2 per cent of the personal income tax for the purposes of this fund.
To establish that this was essentially so and that this vastly improved benefit scheme was provided without extra specific taxes on the public as a whole I want to quote from the Canadian Tax Foundation which in its review entitled "National Finances, 1958-59" at page 84, confirms what I have said in these words:
In general these rates-
For old age security.
-represented the earmarking of a part of existing taxes rather than the establishment of new imposts.
That, I point out, is the contrast between what was done then and what is proposed in this legislation. The additional burden of taxation at that time was negligible. The major source of financing therefore came to the fund from a transfer of taxes rather than from an increase in taxes that were already being imposed in the country. In subsequent years there were deficits, I admit, but in the year 1956-57 the fund was almost in balance.
I think the deficit that year was only $7,500,000, which hon. members will recognize is negligible in relation to the portion that it was always expected would come from general government revenues.
In the budget of March, 1957 there was proposed an increase of $6 per month in the basic pension. Of course later in 1957 there was an additional increase and that increase, together with the $6 increase, made it obvious that the deficit would be considerably increased. But the point I want to emphasize today is that between March, 1957 and the next assembly of this parliament the people of this country, in an election campaign, were told that it would be possible by miracle or otherwise to provide extra pensions out of this fund without any increase in taxation. We have heard even in this debate, and I am not going to document the quotations-and we heard the Prime Minister not only in 1957 but subsequently thereto, and he was just repeating what he said in 1953-say that it was possible to reduce taxes by $500 million-

Old Age Security Act

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.
-and balance the budget and provide extra social welfare benefits.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: He did not say that.

In the fall of 1957,
although this parliament was sitting, we were not the ones to get the announcement. The Prime Minister went to the television audience and told it of his intentions with respect to the additional increase of $9 in the basic pension rate. In June, shortly after assuming office, the Minister of Finance told this country that it was his intention to have a new look at the finances of the country and as a result to have a budget in the session that was called in the fall of 1957. We know that did not develop. We know now why it did not develop. It was obvious to the administration that the miracles they talked about were not likely to prove possible of performance, and as a result we had no budget at the time that legislation was provided for the increase in benefits from this fund.
The position of the Liberal party was made very clear by the then leader of the official opposition, the former prime minister, Mr. St. Laurent, who on October 16, 1957 at page 44 of Hansard said this:
As for the measures forecast to increase old age security and other social benefits, naturally every true Liberal will welcome them in principle. Our sole concern will be to see how they fit into the whole financial picture and how far the government will take effective measures to control the rise in the cost of living which, if unchecked, could easily take away all the advantages of the proposed increases.
Well, the increase, of course, did involve the solvency of the fund, as we now see it clearly, in a very substantial deficit. The Minister of Finance was one of those who, as I say, was a member of the original committee. He was well acquainted with the views of the committee, and there was not too much disagreement among the members of the committee despite their party allegiance. When this legislation came up these were his views with respect to this particular fund; I refer to what he had to say in 1951.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: What is the page?
It was in 1951, on the old age security debate.

speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext: Pages 609 and 610.

It was in October, and this is what the minister had to say at that time:
In the second place, I think that the house will desire to preserve-as the committee recommended in paragraph 64 which I have just read-the consciousness on the part of the individual of the association between the contribution he is making

to the cost and the benefit he is to receive. It is on that basis that rest our ideas, our beliefs in the house, that we are departing as far as we can from the idea of any handout, any payment as of grace, and are seeking to supplant that type of payment with a payment which will be received by the pensioner as of right.
I think the house will be glad to see that the minister-
That is the present hon. member for Essex East. I continue:
-in his proposals, has recommended that the entire cost ... is to come out of the special old age security fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I think the minister referred to was the minister of finance at that time. It was he who brought in the financial proposals for providing the revenues for the fund.
That is right.
Mr. Abbott spoke, of course, right after the minister of national revenue-
I spoke right after him.

-who introduced the proposals, the financial portion of which was referred to by the minister of finance. I continue:
We are subscribing as a house, I take it, to the principle of a pay as you go measure, a pay as you go universal scheme.
Well, if those were the minister's views so strongly and clearly expressed, as he always did express his opinions in those days, I ask what happened to him in December of 1957, when he had full information as Minister of Finance, and had all the calculations, all the forecasts that would be available and decided that it was not desirable or appropriate at that time to tell the public what the cost would be. I am not saying that at that time, if there were some storm warnings, it would have been desirable to do what the minister is doing now, namely have a real over-all increase in the actual rates paid by the individual taxpayers. But if the minister was consistent and still held the views that he so strongly expressed in 1951, I say it was his duty to inform the house of the likely effect upon the fund and to do what was done in 1952, namely allocate from existing taxes the additional amount that would be required to keep this fund in balance.
That, I think, is the important thing that was not done. We know why it was not done. It was not done because there was no desire to let the public know that this could not be done as a result of surpluses available, which they talked about, $500 million, and

other things which we heard so much about not only in the 1957 election campaign but later.
The ministry had very much in their minds the fact that they probably would soon be in another election campaign, and in consequence the bill is coming up only now.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I ask the hon. member a question. Can he tell me why Mr. Harris, when faced with the same question in the spring of 1957, did not propose to deal with the measures required to meet the cost of the additional $6 per month which he was then proposing?

I am familiar with that because I remember the discussions that took place. First of all, we were in boom times and revenues were flourishing. I gave the minister the figure for the best result in any of the previous five years-a small deficit in the fund only $7.5 million. For the year ended March 1957, which had just concluded, the fund was almost in balance, and I do not think an increase of an additional 1 per cent in each particular tax category would have been practicable. Had an increase been made at that time from 2 per cent to 3 per cent in each category the fund actually would have been put into a surplus position based on the expectations of revenue at that time, and that was never the intention of the fund.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Would the hon.
member permit another question. How then did the Liberal government propose to meet the additional cost of the $6 increase, which amounted to over $60 million for a full year?

Having come to the point where the deficit in the fund was only $7 million, and the requirements out of general tax revenues for the old age security program were so much less than had existed even before this legislation, it did not seem unreasonable that by the end of 1958 the anticipated revenues would have kept to normal levels the proportion of contributions from general revenues.
Another matter that I think is very interesting in this connection is the question of the reduction in the actual purchasing power of the pension since it was introduced on January 1, 1952. I have looked at the cost of living figures and at January 1, 1952, the figure was 118.2. In June, 1957 after a period of five and one half years, it had reached 121.6. I calculate that to mean a reduction in the purchasing power of the pension of $1.12 per month. I give this figure after a period of five and one half years, and I now give the figure covering something less than two years of the new administration. During that time the cost of living 66968-9-223
Old Age Security Act
index went up to the extent that the equivalent real value of the old age pension has declined by $1.70. That was part of the thinking in March, 1957. So I emphasize that the real net value of the $9 increase, after taking into account the rise in the cost of living in this period of less than two years, works out to about 17 per cent-

speakerposition: Minister Without Portfolio
speechtext:
May I ask
the hon. member a question?

May I conclude first- but for this 17 per cent increase the purchasing power of the cheque of the old age pensioner there is proposed in this legislation an increase of 50 per cent in the actual taxes that are to be levied for it. This is not a matter of merely making a transfer from the general tax rate to the fund without an over-all increase with respect to the individual taxpayer, as was done in 1952, but it is a completely new and additional 50 per cent rise in the amount of taxes that it is recommended be provided for this fund.
Could I ask the hon. gentleman on what amount of pension he has worked out the $1.12 and on what amount of pension he worked out the $1.70?

I refer to the $9 increase, and if my hon. friend will apply that to the $46 rate he will find it is roughly 20 per cent. My point is that in less than two years the actual purchasing power through inflation has been reduced by the percentage I gave-and down to 17 per cent.
From the $55?
It is $9 on the $46.
But the $1.70 comes off the $55, not off the $9.

The $1.70 certainly is related to the $9 because it is the $9 that was so blatantly advertised as the increase. The result is that, having regard to the reduced purchasing power, the amount of the pension went up net only 17 per cent, and we are now being asked to provide 50 per cent more in contributions to the fund by the taxpayers.
I think that sets out in essence, Mr. Speaker, the difference between what this government is asking and what was done in 1952. In 1952 practically no additional taxation was imposed on the Canadian people as a result of this very big step, as was thought at the time, in improving and enlarging our social security program for the aged. It was done by transfer. This time it is being done

Old Age Security Act
wholly by an increase ot 50 per cent in the actual new rates that will be paid by those who benefit.

Mr. Speaker, I do not think anyone can quarrel too much with the minister for levying new taxation if such new taxation is necessary for the welfare of the people of Canada. However, in this particular case, as was mentioned on another occasion, the old age pensioners of Canada seem to be getting the blame for the new taxes that are to be levied at the present time. They are being advised that the old age security fund is losing money and that the books have to be brought into balance, even though I do not believe it was ever the intention of parliament that the books of the old age security fund should be brought into balance. It was always recognized that there would be many people in receipt of old age pensions who, for various reasons, had not paid very much into the fund in their lifetimes, and therefore it would only be reasonable to expect that for a goodly number of years at least lump sum payments would have to be made from the consolidated revenue fund to the old age security fund in order to balance the books.
I have in mind one particular category of those who receive $55 a month. Under the amendments introduced approximately a year ago any person 70 years of age or over who has been in Canada for as little as ten years is entitled to receive $55 a month. It is obvious that a person who has only lived here for ten years will not have paid nearly as much into the fund as the average Canadian who has paid into the fund over a working lifetime of 30 or 35 years.
So the plea that this additional taxation is necessary in order to balance the books is not valid. Rather, we contend that it is a new plea which has been introduced in order to justify a new imposition and, as the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River has pointed out, it is a heavy increase in taxation. It amounts to an increase of 50 per cent, and if such an increase were applied in other places there certainly would be very serious repercussions. I can well imagine what would happen if the minister were to raise income taxes by 50 per cent or if he were to raise corporation taxes by 50 per cent. However, when it comes to putting the responsibility on the old age pensioners of Canada, we find that we have a government in office which is willing to blame them for a tax rise as great as 50 per cent.
We are just wondering on this Monday, Mr. Speaker, whether these tax increases are

at all necessary. After all, we have been reading our week-end newspapers and listening to the radio, and we know that a certain prime minister made a speech in Montreal over the week end in which he forecast a fantastic improvement in the Canadian economic situation over the balance of this year, at least. He did not have too much to say about the year after.
However, if improvement on the economic scene is going to take place, as was predicted by the Prime Minister, then one would imagine that the old rates would have supplied the Minister of Finance with sufficient revenue so the additional tax imposts would have been looked upon as unnecessary. I have no doubt that the Minister of Finance has also read the Prime Minister's speech delivered last week end in Montreal. I was expecting him, at this sitting of parliament, to say that in the light of the prediction by the Prime Minister over the week end the government was now asking the consent of the house to withdraw the bill now before us. The whole attitude surrounding the new bill is certainly a far cry from the new kind of deal the pensioners of Canada were led to believe they would get. They were informed clearly that the $9 per month added pension was only the beginning.
We now have the Clark report filed, and so far as we can gather from the replies to questions on the orders of the day the Clark report has been truly filed. In fact the house may never even get a chance to consider the Clark report. The new deal seems to be to put the blame for the 50 per cent increase on certain already onerously taxed people of Canada. In the case of the sales tax there is an increase of 10 per cent. We find this position very difficult to reconcile. On the one hand we have the Prime Minister saying the economy is going to move forward at such a rapid pace that we would expect the minister to be in receipt of a great deal of added revenue, and on the other hand the minister says he regrets that because of the deficit in the pension fund, he must levy this unusually heavy, 50 per cent increase in taxation.
If the minister's argument that this is necessary in order to bring the fund into balance is true, then Mr. Speaker, the minister is also introducing a new principle. This will confirm the fact that henceforth old age pensions are a matter of right. This also confirms the claim that has long been made by many old age pensioners, that they are entitled to this money inasmuch as they are the ones who have paid for it. If that is the case, then the minister is very remiss in that he does not allow these pensioners to

decide when and where in the world they are going to spend their money. If the minister is going to put this fund in balance, if the minister is claiming that it shall be self-liquidating, then the people who are in receipt of their own savings ought to be at liberty to determine where they are going to spend the money. They should have the right to spend it anywhere in the world.
I regret very much this increase in taxation, and especially do I regret the blame being put where it is. We feel that if the economy had not been in a period of recession this added impost would not have been found necessary. We find that once again the minister, by his acts, is admitting that conditions in the country are not as they were claimed to be last week end by the Prime Minister. We would suppose that rather than adopt these added imposts, the government should seriously consider how they could increase revenues by expanding the economy of the country as a whole.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Leader of the Opposition):
speakerposition: Leader of the Official Opposition
speechtext:
The bill before us is a bill to meet the bills. In so far as the attitude of the official opposition toward the principle involved in the bill is concerned, that has been clearly stated by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River. I desire to add only a word or two to what he has said. In so far as the principle of the legislation is concerned, and the benefits involved in old age pensions, as my hon. friend has said our former leader, Mr. St. Laurent, explained our position on October 16, 1957. Our position now is as it was then. He said then that every true Liberal will welcome in principle this increase in old age security and other social benefits, but our concern, as he said then and it is our concern now, is to see how they fit into our financial picture.
We know now how they fit into that picture because, as has been pointed out, the increase in benefits which necessitated this bill, the real increase having regard to the increased cost of living, is 17 per cent and the taxation increase is 50 per cent. Economic considerations have now made it necessary, therefore, for the government to take the kind of action which party political considerations prevented them from taking only a year ago, when it should have been taken. As a result the sales tax is now at the highest level in our history.
This must be of interest to the minister, in view of what he said in the past about sales tax, and I refer to the debate in 1951 from which my hon. friend has already quoted. The present Minister of Finance stated, as reported on page 610 of Hansard for November 1, 1951:
We must recognize as well that it is a costly tax to the consumer because it pyramids as the result 66968-9-223i
Old Age Security Act
of mark-ups as the goods pass from hand to hand, from the manufacturer or producer, who pays the tax in the first instance, to the wholesaler, from the wholesaler to the retailer, from the retailer to the consumer, and that a 2 per cent sales tax-
That is what we were talking about then.
-in this way levied on the manufacturer or producer will probably cost the consumer not 2 per cent but closer to 4 per cent on the cost of the goods that he has to buy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, we are proposing to increase this tax from 2 per cent to 3 per cent. The position of our party on this matter is clear. We think the government is to be condemned for its refusal to apply the pay as you go principle in the fall of 1957, when it increased the pension without increasing the contributions and at a time-this is in contrast to the situation which prevailed in the spring-when a deficit was as certain as anything could be. The increase could have been made and should have been made at that time, having regard to the economic picture, by transferring receipts from existing taxes to the fund. This was the best method at the time of keeping it in reasonable balance.
At that time, Mr. Speaker, party considerations took precedence over economic considerations. So far as we are concerned we do not want to share the blame now, because we would have approached the whole problem in a different way then. The government took full responsibility before the election for the political decisions which have led to the present financial difficulties. It must now, therefore, accept full financial responsibility for the measures that have to be taken to get the country out of these difficulties, and this bill is the reflection of one difficulty. I think we can leave it at that.

Mr. Speaker, I do not want to delay the house, because, as I say,
I find that except for the amendments of last week the bill appears in the form of which notice was given, and the public would have every expectation of the things in the bill as a result of the minister's budget address of April 9. But I did feel the other evening that I had overlooked a comment which I would very much have liked to have made when we were discussing the Customs Tariff, and I refer to the fact that we have recently lost, I guess, our very distinguished former chairman of the board. I would like to pay my compliments to him. He is a man who has served under five prime ministers, and I think even the present minister asked him to continue a little beyond the time when he might have otherwise wanted to have had some leisure.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Twice.

Twice. We have in Canada some very sterling servants of the public, and I do not think any of them have more general admiration than is held for him by people not only in Canada but in places abroad.
I have found tariff a most intricate and difficult subject to study. I think it is even more difficult than certain presentations to the courts. Usually in courts we have only two conflicting opinions; but anyone who peruses the very exceptionally exhaustive reports of the tariff board in recent years will understand that in an economy such as ours the board is not considering the conflicting desires and economic interests of merely two litigants appealing to the board, but in many cases perhaps half a dozen or more in more or less conflict. In other words, the judicial and sensible decisions which have to be resolved are extremely onerous indeed. I think that both governments have followed the recommendations of this board fairly closely. Certainly the minister did last year, and I realize that he went a long way this time to accept the recommendations of the tariff board in that very intricate study of fruits and vegetables. This was not quite so simple as in other reports. Sometimes the Minister of Finance if he chooses can actually take the suggested amendments to the tariff

schedules as recommended by the board without much personal contribution to policy. But in this case the minister and his officials in the department had treaty obligations to a number of countries, and they had to relate the recommendations of the board with those involved treaty obligations. I should also like to pay my respects to other members of the tariff board some of whom are retiring at this time. Perhaps during the committee stage we shall be able to refer to others, in front of the minister, right now. I think of Mr. Glass who has been made a member of the board-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: And vice chairman.

And vice chairman. I had reason over the years to consult him quite frequently in seeking his counsel and advice on these matters which are so detailed and complicated. I did not consult him or anybody else in the minister's department this year, because I thought the changes taking place were uprooting and I was not quite sure what the result will be. I know the minister will be equally well served in the department in having Dr. Annis as Mr. Glass' successor. We have exceptionally devoted civil servants engaged in a most exacting task, and quite irrespective of party politics I think the minister will agree that they are most deserving of recognition by this house and by the country.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I quite agree.

The minister will have noticed that the committee on estimates has concluded a very interesting course of meetings with the officials of the Department of National Revenue. It was hard to draw the line, sometimes, between those who administer our customs laws and the Minister of Finance who actually has to recommend the customs rates which shall prevail. However, I did note that in paragraph 1 of the committee's report there was a suggestion that it be made mandatory that all goods from outside Canada should be labelled. Perhaps the minister could make some comment on that when he replies, if he has an opportunity.
I take it that we shall in committee be able to be our own judges on the matter of procedure, and while there is no desire to be repetitive and to go over individual items, there are items in the schedule which, after a few days' lapse, do require, perhaps, some further clarification. I am sure the minister will make that possible at the committee stage. I do not wish to alarm the minister, and I hasten to say that there are not many items which this group is proposing to follow up, having regard to less formal discussion we had in committee last week. But I should
Customs Tariff
like to direct a few questions to the minister about the new category of machines which are deemed to be made in Canada. Am I right in thinking that this could properly be done on the committee stage, on the schedule?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

Although the items which have been subject to increases in this budget are, for the most part, or in large part, not items with which many people in the public are familiar, I think it has been understood that the over-all emphasis was on increasing protection again. Certainly, with respect to machines, we are simply returning to precedents that were followed when we last had a Conservative government, and once again we have something which is in the nature of a legalistic and arbitrary determination of what is made in Canada, without the usual adjudication by officials of the department and the courts. It is true that if any taxpayer is aggrieved he has the right to appeal to the tariff board and, in succession, to the exchequer court and to the Supreme Court of Canada. I think this is another matter which we can discuss further on the committee stage.
The section having to do with woollen goods, as we predicted last year, is likely to have repercussions among some of our better customers-people to whom we export goods in excess of the imports which are to be subject to the new duties. Again, I think this is a matter which can appropriately be discussed in committee.
In conclusion, I might mention, as I did the other day, that the minister and his officials have helped the house considerably by the actual new grouping of the schedules and by the explanatory remarks which were made on April 9 which led the average member of parliament to a better understanding of the appropriate occasion on which to debate these items, which is usually on the schedules. I will leave it to the minister to decide later whether or not we should call each item individually or whether we shall deal with them in a broad group.

If no one else wishes to speak, I want to say about three sentences in order to express once again the very strong objection which I feel to this regrettable increase in the wool tariff. This objection is shared, I believe by everyone engaged in the fishing industry. I think it is also probably shared by primary producers in the wheat growing areas of this country.
The minister referred to it as a modest increase. That is his favourite word, and one which he uses in connection with almost every impost. He says they are modest increases, implying that they are of no use

Customs Tariff
as protection measures. But it is quite obvious that the government would not have made these changes at all if they had not been expected to keep out goods. Certainly, the minister has never argued that this particular change is a revenue-producing one, and it seems to me this is a retrograde step for a trading country such as Canada to take when we depend so much on maintaining our exports to countries abroad.
The minister may be right in saying that its effect on the cost of living may be very small, but practically everything which this government has done since taking office two years ago has tended to increase the cost of living as well as the cost of production of primary producers. This is another stage in that direction and it seems to me to be regrettable on that account, also.

speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I do not regard six days as haste in the light of experience in some other years. In that light this is quite a long time to have elapsed between the resolution stage and the stage of second reading of the bill with respect to tariff changes where the bill simply follows the language of the resolution precisely.

Mr. Chairman, this is the first opportunity we have had to ask the minister a question or two on this subject. I notice that this is not a significant item with respect to a change in the receipts of the Minister of Finance; however, he does expect to collect $3 million more in customs tariff as the result of these amendments he is now proposing.
As the hon. member for Bonavista-Twil-lingate mentioned earlier, it is obvious that ever since this government took office every time it has introduced amendments to the Customs Tariff the net effect has been the raising of the tariff against products from other countries entering Canada. I should like the minister to give the committee an indication of what steps he has taken since he became Minister of Finance toward obtaining a reversal of this tendency.
The minister has made numerous references to commonwealth meetings on economic matters. I believe a meeting was held in Montreal a year ago. Has the minister or the government ever made any proposals to other commonwealth countries, NATO countries or other countries adhering to GATT that would tend to liberalize world trade and especially that would liberalize trade as between members of the commonwealth, members within NATO or the member nations of GATT? If so, what has been the reaction of these countries to such a proposal? If a proposal of this nature has been made why has it not been carried out? Why has the minister followed this process of asking parliament to amend the act each year the net result of which is to curtail the free flow of trade between nations?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the increase in revenue from the customs tariff is expected from the customs duty on liquor and that alone. As I indicated in the budget speech, we do not expect any appreciable difference in receipts of revenues from customs duties in respect of the other changes.

The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam is completely wrong in talking about the trend and the result of this year's tariff proposals. I will give it for the third time. I gave it in my budget speech, full details of which appear at page 2422 of Hansard of April 9 in the second column. I repeated this in the discussion in the committee of ways and means on May 5 but I shall be quite happy to give it again. I said that with respect to the changes proposed in the tariffs this year that 142 tariff items and sub-items are affected by the resolutions. In the case of 32 items the rates of duty are being increased. In the case of 40 items rates are being reduced. In the case of 9 items, all involving fruits and vegetables, rates are being both increased and decreased depending on the season. I concluded by saying that there are 61 items for which rates of duty are left unchanged and for which the changes proposed are, for the most part, purely formal.
So far as GATT is concerned, there will be a GATT meeting shortly and negotiations will proceed there. There will be GATT negotiations again in the autumn and also in 1960. These occur from time to time. Within the course of these negotiations, whenever we ask for an increase in a bound rate we are asked to give compensation in some other form, sometimes in the form of decreases. This process of negotiation with consequent increases and decreases has become almost a continuous process due to the frequency of the meetings of GATT.

Mr. Chairman, the minister says I am completely wrong. He claims he has increased the customs tariff on 32 items and decreased it on 40 items and that we are therefore, ipso facto, bound to assume he has lowered the rates when he has in fact done nothing of the kind. It all depends on which items are raised or lowered. May I refer the minister to his own remarks in the budget address on April 9 last at page 2414 of Hansard. In table 3 on that page he indicates that his receipts from customs tariffs in the year 1958-59 are forecast as being $486 million. In the following fiscal year ending March 31, 1960-and this was before the currently proposed tax changes-he anticipates revenue from this source in the amount of $525 million. Therefore in one year the minister expects a rise in income under the customs tariff of $39 million.
I am aware of the fact that his anticipated increase because of the bill now before us is not very large. He records that on page 2425 of Hansard, and he indicates that he expects that in a full year his income in regard to these changes will grow by only $3 million.
Customs Tariff
However, we had this a year ago, Mr. Chairman, when the house was informed that there really is not much of a change here. Many items are being reduced and the tariff on a lesser number of items is being raised. However, it all depends on the volume of imports of those items as to whether or not the cost of living of the Canadian people is really being raised. I cannot let the minister get away with saying that I am completely wrong. His income under the customs tariff has been rising since he became minister and since these amendments have been introduced. The hon. member for Bonavista-Twillingate was perfectly right when he said that the over-all effect of customs tariff changes since this government has taken office has been a rise in the amount of tariff that the Canadian people have to pay.
I was pleased to note that the minister said there would be many more meetings of GATT. However, the minister gave us no indication that his government is planning any proposals to the member nations under GATT that would lead to a lowering of tariffs. The minister indicated that each time they meet there is a demand made for the raising of some tariffs but no proposal on the part of his government to reduce them. The minister also completely ignored my request for a report of the meeting of the commonwealth economic conference which was held last fall, the object of which was supposed to be to enhance trade within the commonwealth. Presumably one of the methods that would be employed to enhance the exchange of commodities between commonwealth countries would be by rather severe amendments to the existing customs tariffs acts of the various commonwealth members. I hope that at this time the minister will indicate some of the results in this regard that have emanated from the Montreal economic conference, which was an important conference.

Perhaps the committee would like an explanation of this item, Mr. Chairman. This is a matter that was brought to my attention by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni since it was before the committee of ways and means and reported back to the house on Tuesday last, May 5. He brought forward representations also received from the British Columbia loggers association in this respect.
The effect of the amendment which is now proposed is to withdraw a proposed change which had been introduced in the budget at the request of the Canadian automobile chamber of commerce. The objective was to simplify the administrative procedure in importing certain parts of logging trucks. It was brought to my attention by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, however, that the change might have some adverse and, I may say, completely unintended effects upon the Canadian logging industry. Tariff item

411a covers certain equipment used in logging operations. This item carries a mostfavoured-nation rate of 12J per cent and imports under it are exempt from sales tax. The purpose in proposing that tariff item 411a be enumerated in the automobile parts items was to provide entry for such parts as were ruled not to be made in Canada either free of duty or at a most-favoured-nation rate of 7J per cent.
It now appears, however, that while the original amendment would have had this effect it would also raise questions as to the continued exemption of such parts from the sales tax, and it was certainly not our intention to deprive these parts of the exemption they now enjoy in respect of sales tax. Therefore the amendment now proposed will have the effect of restoring the position which existed prior to the budget both as to the rates of duty and the application of sales tax, and further consideration will be given during the course of the next year to this whole situation.
I may say that since the hon. member for Comox-Alberni brought this matter to my attention we have communicated with the Canadian automobile chamber of commerce and they are not offering any objections to the amendment now proposed. I should like to express my very warm thanks to the hon. member for Comox-Alberni for bringing this matter to my attention as he has done. It was, I think, a very useful service that he rendered to me as well as a very useful service to the British Columbia logging industry.

Mr. Chairman, I should like to say a word of thanks to the minister for the prompt action he took when I brought this problem to him. He did not have much time. It was only a matter of hours. I appreciate and I am certain that the industry in British Columbia appreciates the action he took so promptly.

Customs Tariff
which we will come to in a moment, is to increase the price here, and presumably therefore, since this was supposed to be a matter of negotiation, in order to give some advantage to the other country in exchange for the woollen increases the government had some kind of argument to offer as to what advantage would go to the Italians.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: This item is of principal interest to Italian exporters and they have not required any instruction on the part of Canada as to what the value of a reduction in the tariff on these items may mean to them. There have been negotiations and in the course of those negotiations they have put whatever value they think is proper on this particular concession.
Were these things asked for by the Italians or were they offered by us?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It is very difficult to separate any particular time in the course of negotiations and say when something was initiated. The negotiations with the Italian government representatives in regard to these changes in the tariffs so far as they were of interest to Italy have been going on for some time. This particular change has taken place in the course of the negotiations. It was regarded by the representatives of the Italian government as something of interest to them and, as the committee is aware, the tariff proposal will have the effect of reducing the British preferential and most-favoured-nation duties by 30 per cent, that is, from 80 per cent to 50 per cent. I do not need to tell hon. members that most of the types of wines imported under this item are not produced in Canada.

I think it is pretty obvious that none of them is except I believe there is a kind of vermouth produced in the Niagara peninsula. I do not know whether that is the kind the minister uses. But the minister must realize that as far as I am aware-it may be that I am wrongly informed but I believe it is true-in every province I know anything about there is a monopoly in the sale of these products by an agency of the provincial government, and even if the duty were reduced to nothing the advantage would be nil to the exporting country unless there was some assurance that the reduction in duty was not simply going to be put into the provincial treasury but was going to be passed on to the consumer. With the exception of our marble imports from Italy which I cannot imagine are very extensive, although I intend to ask about them later, it would appear that the only concessions that were offered to the Italians for the injury we were

proposing to do to their exports of woollens involved the commodities in items 162 and 163, items which to the best of my knowledge are controlled by monopolies in every province. There may be one province in which that is not true. I am very surprised that the minister is not informed as to how it was that the Italians were satisfied, which I doubt, with concessions of this character.
I would urge the minister to be a little more frank with us and tell us what arguments were used in this context.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the Italians are quite capable of defending their own interests in any negotiations. I do not think it is the duty of any Canadian to suggest that they should ask more in the way of concessions than they thought, in the course of these negotiations, they should ask.

I am not suggesting that they should ask more, but I happen to represent a constituency which has a very valuable market in Italy for one of the two products produced in that constituency, namely salt codfish. This market, in my opinion, is likely to be jeopardized by these changes in part III. Although the minister has never shown much interest in that section of the country or in that community, it does seem to those of us who represent this area that we should have the right to have our questions answered.
We have an interest in seeing that a good customer, Italy-in fact, we have not in recent years been able to satisfy the demand of the Italians for this product-should not be lost by tariff action taken by this government. I have no apology whatever, for this reason, for pressing for assurance about this matter. Moreover, as the minister well knows, the establishment of a common market has brought Italy and France, into a very close relationship. France has become a very serious competitor of Canada in the world market for salt codfish. There is every reason to be apprehensive about this Italian market.
It does not seem to me that it is incumbent upon the government in making tariff changes to see that they do not injure a community like the fishing community which has to sell its products in an export market or not at all and which, from a consumer's point of view, is a captive market for other industries in Canada which do benefit from the protective tariffs. I do not think it is unreasonable at all to expect the Minister of Finance, when asking us to change the tariff structure of this country to the apparent detriment of one industry and one section of the country, to give us assurances that he satisfied this valuable customer of ours that these changes

were not going to injure his capacity to buy these primary products of Canada such as fish and wheat.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: We were over all this in the committee of ways and means. I dealt with this subject and gave the hon. member a full explanation. He is just asking me to repeat it.

I am not asking the minister to repeat. The minister keeps saying that we have been over all these things, but he gives no explanation and no answer. He does not deal with any of the questions that we ask. The minister seems to forget that it is not so many years since he sat over here and I predict it will not be so many years before he will be back here, especially if he treats parliament in the way in which he has been treating it lately.
When we are raising the tariff structure of this country we are entitled to know why these things are being done, and to know that some Canadian interests and industries are not being injured by these changes. In my opinion this change is a most retrograde step and is very detrimental to this country in every respect. It is most unfortunate it was made at all. It does seem to me we are entitled, at least, to be told some serious effort was made to get some assurances that Canadian producers who do have to stand all the cold hard winds of international trade are not to be injured any more than can possibly be avoided. If the government intends, as I know they do, to persist in this unfortunate course they have undertaken, then we are entitled to this information.

He said: Mr. Speaker, on second reading of Bill No. C-43, to amend the Unemployment Insurance Act, I wish to make a few observations. The present amendments in this bill will provide coverage for a greater number of wage earners. They will increase benefits and allowable earnings. They will also increase contributions. They will extend the benefit period to 52 weeks.
Today, in asking the house to give consideration to these amendments I would refer first to section 3 of the bill. This section raises the wage ceiling on insurability, bringing in under the umbrella of unemployment insurance protection persons making up to $5,460 as compared with only $4,800 under the present act.
I should also like to explain that we have adopted a new principle in regard to allowable earnings as shown in the table on page 6 of the bill. Hon. members will note that the benefit rate for a person with a dependant is higher than that for a person without a dependant, even though their wages may have been the same. This is the way in which the act recognizes the greater responsibilities of those with dependants. At the present time, however, this principle is not recognized in the allowable earnings schedule. We propose, therefore, a new schedule that provides for somewhat higher allowable earnings for the person with a dependant.
Furthermore, since the allowable earnings idea was first incorporated in the act in 1955 experience has shown that the amount of earnings allowed should be higher if the claimant is to have adequate incentive to take on casual work. We propose, therefore, to make the allowable earnings one-half of the claimant's weekly benefit rate, rounded to the nearest dollar. By doing this, we will be producing two desirable results with one amendment; that is, we will be recognizing the greater responsibilities of those with dependants and we will also be putting a realistic price tag on incentive to work.
Unemployment Insurance Act
I should like to deal now with the new schedule of benefit rates. This schedule appears on page four of the bill. It will be noted that two new classes of benefits are added, one a new maximum of $36 for a person with one dependent, earning $69 a week and over; another of $33 for a person with one dependent earning between $63 and $70 per week. Previously persons earning over $57 weekly could not draw more than $30. That was the maximum. The two new clauses display a more realistic regard for present economic conditions. Also, in increasing the schedule of allowable earnings all the way along the line, the maximum total income now permitted to an unemployed person with one dependent is $54 per week compared with the previous $43 per week. Thus, in order to provide a higher benefit range we have had to provide for increased contributions.
In connection with this I should point out to hon. members that during the last two winters of moderate recession, which Canada suffered along with a great number of other countries, the drain on the fund has been heavy. In 1957-58 outgo from the fund was in the neighbourhood of $385 million. For 1958-59 the figure will be higher. In the two past years the fund has been reduced by almost $400 million. No one will deny that this has been a heavy drain. On the other hand, Mr. Speaker, I do not think that anyone would quarrel with this use of the fund for the purpose for which the fund was originally set up.
The expenditures that were made from the fund in the past two years were made for the purpose of easing the lot of those whose misfortune it was to fall into unemployment. The amendments which are now before you will make possible further easement of that difficult and unpleasant situation, while at the same time keeping the fund on a sound basis. I would point out at the same time that we do not anticipate a need for drains on the fund in the immediate future of the magnitude of those of the past two years. All signs now point to a steady strengthening of the economy. However, there is a responsibility on the government to maintain the fund in a condition of equilibrium and this the new schedule of contributions will help materially in effecting.
I now come to an amendment which deserves notice at this time. I refer to section 10 of the bill which sets out the grounds on which the period of qualification may be extended and adds to these grounds time served in penitentiary up to two years. Ordinarily a person who had spent up to two years in penitentiary, would lose the benefit of unemployment insurance contributions, which

Unemployment Insurance Act would impose a further punishment in addition to those levied by the court. This disability is now removed and it will help a great deal in the rehabilitation of those who have been unfortunate enough to have punishment imposed upon them by the courts.
The final major amendment increases the maximum duration of benefit from 36 weeks to 52 weeks. This is being introduced in answer to many representations and reverts to the situation that existed back in 1955 prior to the time when there was a general revision and amendments were made to the act.

speechtext:
I welcome that suggestion which I think is a good one because of the character of the bill. However, that does not remove, of course, the fact that there are a number of very important considerations of principle and related circumstances that can more appropriately be discussed on second reading as I now propose to do. I thank the minister for tabling that report about which I propose to have something to say during the course of my remarks. I regret that I cannot treat it as he treats it, as a document confidential to the members of the advisory committee and the minister.
I think it is very important at the outset of the discussion that we should not forget that the unemployment insurance commission and its auxiliary and related bodies were enacted by statute to occupy a rather unique position, certainly different from the functions assigned to the various divisions of a particular department. The unemployment insurance commission is a body that reports, through the Minister of Labour (Mr. Starr), to the governor in council. There is nothing in the act that authorizes the advisory committee to report directly to the minister. However, as I said at the outset I will have more to say on that subject as I proceed.
The minister dealt cursorily with certain features of the bill. He referred to the fact that increased rates were going to be imposed on the main contributing bodies, employers and employees, and also a consequential increase in the grant provided by Canada out of the consolidated revenue fund. Then he said that there would also be increased benefits. I must say that I have carefully perused the legislation and I think it is a very strong overstatement to say that the bill provides for any real increase in benefits. It does make certain provision for extension of the present period to 52 weeks, restoring the old situation, but generally speaking the bill does not provide for any increases in the rates of benefit.
What this bill does is to impose on the workers and the employers a heavy increased obligation, an obligation which in its totality represents further taxation of these

two segments of the community in an amount of money equal to almost one-third of the additional burden of taxation imposed by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) in his budget. What we are now dealing with is a measure that is going to impose an additional tax burden on the workers and the employers, a burden that was not referred to by the Minister of Finance when he presented his budget to us on April 9.
It is true that in his budget speech he made reference to the unemployment insurance fund. He referred to the fact that as a result of unemployment in the country there had been an impairment of the integrity of that fund. No reference was made by him, however, and no detailed reference was made today by the Minister of Labour to indicate what this particular measure will mean in terms of additional contributions by two groups in our national community. This should be viewed in the light of the fact that the measure, as I say, does not provide for any real increase in benefits to those who are called upon to make the contributions provided for by this act.
The minister, and I think understandably from his point of view, did not deal with a matter to which I referred on the resolution stage. I do not want to revive that matter, but I do want to indicate to the minister that in my judgment, as well as in the judgment of those who sit on Mr. Speaker's left, we are not satisfied that the Unemployment Insurance Act has been complied with in so far as the appointment of Mr. MacArthur is concerned in succession to Mr. Tallon. I repeat that there is nothing against Mr. MacArthur whatever in terms of confidence. I believe that what the minister has said, and the evidence before us, clearly indicates that there has not been a proper consultation with labour as required by the Unemployment Insurance Act.
The minister indicated when he spoke the other day on the resolution, and I refer to his words at page 3361 of Hansard for May 5, 1959, that the reason for this bill is to maintain the fund in a situation of stability over the next few years. He said that during the past two years of recession which we have experienced there has been a pretty heavy drain on this fund. Those words by the minister, I think, represent the true situation. I would point out that the fund dropped by $134.2 million in 1957-58 and by $247.9 million in 1958-59, a total reduction of $382.1 million in two years. At no time previously had the fund dropped by such a large amount in any one or two years period.
This is, of course, an indication of the level of unemployment we have in this country.
Unemployment Insurance Act One would have thought from the statement made by the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) outside of this house on Friday last that the situation was otherwise when he said that we were emerging from the recession more rapidly than any other country in the western world. Of course, the facts are precisely the opposite, particularly in so far as unemployment is concerned. It is no wonder, then, that there has been a drop in the level of the unemployment insurance fund, the replenishment of which the minister said is the primary objective of this legislation.
Now, the aggregate of the replenishment which the minister has in mind is going to be made up of two elements. First, there will be the contribution that will be made by insured persons whose earnings are in the bracket between the present maximum of $4,800 per annum and the new maximum of $5,460. The second element will be the increased contribution payable by employees and employers as a result of the increase in rates of contribution of those now earning $4,800 or less. The minister told us the other day that as a result of this legislation 80,000 contributors will be brought back into the scheme. I have calculated that each of these, if fully employed, will pay 52 times 94 cents or $44.88 per annum. The total 80,000 additional workers to which my hon. friend referred in this group will contribute annually $4 million more and the employers will contribute a like amount.
Now with regard to the present class that is up to the $4,800 range, the rates of increase vary upward from 25 per cent to 56.7 per cent. It is, of course, difficult to know the present weighting of the different classes. If we assume, however, that the average rate of increase will be 30 per cent, then the employees in this class, that is the $4,800 or less, would pay roughly 30 per cent of the 1957-58 contribution, that is to say $94 million or an aggregate of $28.3 million. If these estimates are correct, or even approximately correct, this new bill will lay additional burdens on the employers of Canada of approximately $32.3 million, and a similar burden on the employees of $32.3 million.
At six o'clock the house took recess.
