subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OP REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I had concluded my remarks before dinner, by observing that this bill would impose an

Unemployment Insurance Act additional burden on the two main contributors, the employers and the employees respectively, in the amount of $32.3 million. I should now like to emphasize that for those who fall into the new class who are not now making any contribution to the unemployment insurance fund, the new measure will subject them to a contribution of $48.88 per annum, which is a substantial amount particularly when one thinks of the increases in sales taxes, corporation tax, income tax and other impositions which were provided for in the recent budget. It certainly imposes a substantial burden on industry which has already been called upon to pay substantial taxes; and of course this represents an important burden now imposed on the workers of our country.
The minister said when he was explaining these proposed increased contributions that the reason was to maintain the fund in stability over the next few years. One might reasonably ask whether the increased contributions do not represent a heavy burden both on industry and the labour force for conditions which have prevailed in the last two years and for which they cannot be held, of course, accountable.
I said when speaking the other night that one of the reasons for the position in which we find the fund is because of invasions made on this fund since the period following June 1957. I indicated that of course hon. gentlemen opposite were not the first to provide for supplementary benefits, but that whenever supplementary benefits had been provided for, as they were on three occasions by the previous administration, steps were taken to replenish the fund. With regard to the two occasions that have presented themselves during the term of the present administration in respect of which there has been an invasion of the fund for the purpose of providing seasonal or supplementary benefits there was no consequential action taken by the government to replenish the fund.
No one quarrels, of course, with the desirability for these supplementary payments, particularly in the last two years when there has been serious unemployment, more serious that at any time since the period between 1930 and 1935. But we have argued in this session and in other sessions that the burden was one that should have been shared by the people of Canada generally and not a burden that should have been imposed only on two segments of the population, namely the employers and the employees. That is obviously a responsibility which should be shared by all Canadians, and to have imposed this obligation on the workers and on the employers without replenishing the fund is in part one


of the reasons why the government and the unemployment insurance commission and the advisory committee have been disturbed about the present state of the fund.
I said that when we invaded the fund for the purpose of providing supplementary benefits we took steps to replenish the fund. That was done in the years 1949-50, 1950-51, and in 1951-52. In 1949-50 vote 585 provided for reimbursement to the fund under section 87 (f) (1) of the act in the amount of $1,500,000. The actual expenditure amounted, however, to only $13,425.56. The following year, vote 597 provided for similar purposes the amount of $1,780,000, which was fully expended. In 1951-52 vote 717 provided for $40,000, of which $35,438.35 was spent.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OP REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, might I ask the hon. member a question. Were these votes to provide for the payment of seasonal benefits which were being granted at the time?

subtopic: AMENDMENTS TO INCREASE RATES OP REMUNERATION AND CONTRIBUTIONS, ETC.
speechtext:
They were consequential upon the fact that the government had recommended to this house legislation providing for supplementary payments, and the government took steps to replenish the fund in accordance with its belief that this was a responsibility which should be shared not just by the workers and the employers but by the people of Canada, generally, through the consolidated fund.
So if the government is faced with a situation where the fund in 1959 has been reduced to $496.3 million as compared with what it was, let us say, in 1954, $881.3 million, one of the contributing reasons is the failure of the government to replenish the fund in accordance with a responsibility that belongs to all Canadians. The government may have had budgetary reasons for that; it may not have wanted to add to the deficit of 1957-58 or the larger deficit of 1958-59. But that certainly does not justify the invasion of a fund contributed to by two groups for the purpose of giving them maintenance grants which they require, as this winter and last fall indicated they did require, in the event of a high level of unemployment. I am sure that in considering the increased contributions which the employers and the employees must make under this measure one cannot help but wonder whether the increased contribution is designed to improve the financial condition of the fund or whether it is designed to pay the true actuarial cost of the additional coverage. I am sure that the minister would have satisfied the house if in his brief statement he had included some explanation for the government's course in this particular.

Mr. Speaker, we all recall some of the words of the Prime Minister (Mr. Diefen-baker) in connection with unemployment insurance. At Port Alberni on March 12, 1958 the leader of the Conservative party, the present Prime Minister, told the audience in that community that when his government came to power in June 1957 there was the greatest unemployment in Canada's history. He was giving them the facts, he said. He told the audience that now we had passed the peak of unemployment in this country. Of course, he did not give the figures, but, Mr. Speaker, you and I know, as do hon. members of this house, that the situation that eventuated after that speech was made is not supported by the facts. The real situation in the measure before the house is clear, that the government did not foresee the situation which now confronts us, and in failing to foresee it did not take the necessary preparatory steps and action to maintain the integrity of the fund.
The Prime Minister said at Pembroke on March 28 that the Liberals were saying unemployment was still on the increase but he said figures from the national employment service showed that registrations for unemployment insurance which had been mounting steadily all winter were finally going down. Registrations, the Prime Minister said, had gone up by 10,000 in the first half of March, but in the week beginning March 20 there had been a drop of 3,120, an indication that Canada's unemployment crisis had passed its peak. That confirms what I have just said, because the figures for March, published late in April, reveal that for the week ending March 22 there were 590,000 persons out of work and seeking jobs-or 10 per cent of the labour force-and 883,660 applicants for employment.
If the fund is in the dangerous state in which those who have to do with this matter obviously regard it to be, a contributing factor is the heavy invasion of it because of the fact that we have had this high level of unemployment in Canada. I suggest to the Minister of Labour that the government should have been warned last year by what was said on this side of the house, and should have taken steps not only to mitigate the occasion of unemployment but also, as was done by its predecessors, to see that the integrity of the fund was maintained in a manner which represented the common contribution of the people of Canada generally.
In the short presentation which he made today, the minister took credit for the value of this legislation in that it is extending the period from 36 weeks to 52 weeks and restoring the situation which prevailed prior to the amendment introduced by Mr. Gregg. The
Unemployment Insurance Act Minister of Labour has not, of course, overlooked the fact that the unemployment insurance commission noted, in the last report but one which it made to parliament, on page 50, that in view of the high percentage of claimants who did not use the long period of entitlement which was often set up for them it was considered justifiable to reduce the period of entitlement. And the commission went on to explain that in certain circumstances a claimant might continue to receive benefit, with or without partial earnings, throughout 51 instead of 36 weeks.
The fact remains that it was indicated from experience that between 1949 and 1953, 9.9 per cent of the claimants drew benefits for 20 weeks or more and consequently it would be a pity if the great mass of contributors were called upon to pay for much longer periods of benefit than they were likely to need. This, of course, was not mentioned by the Minister of Labour. It means that for the very large number of individuals who are outside this 9.9 per cent, a heavy added burden results from the amendments proposed. I do not quarrel with this in principle, except that I think that in regarding this as one of the great advantages of the legislation now before us, the minister should have pointed out the limited number of people who, in the light of experience, are likely to profit from this particular modification of the act.
We were told by the Prime Minister repeatedly, during the election of 1957 in particular, that if his government came to office the waiting period would be eliminated entirely. I think the government should be reminded of that promise as my reading of the bill does not indicate that this particular promise is being fulfilled by the administration.
It is noteworthy that the Canadian Labour Congress has called for compensation on the basis of two-thirds of the earnings of the beneficiaries under this scheme. I took issue with the Minister of Labour at the outset of my remarks by saying that while this measure imposes additional contributions from both employers and employees it does not provide any real increase in benefits. The minister said it does, and I hope that at some point he will indicate what these increased benefits are.
In the light of the present value of our dollar one wonders whether the present level of benefit is satisfactory. One would have thought that if there was to be this additional burden by way of increased rates, to the extent of 30 per cent covering some categories, there would have been some increase in the amount of benefit provided for workers covered by this legislation. There is no
3542	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act doubt that the Unemployment Insurance Act was intended to cover every earning worker, and to provide its benefits for all. That, I am sure, is the intention of the present administration, as it was the intention of its predecessor. It seems to me that the benefits provided by the act should enable a worker to look after himself and his family on a satisfactory basis. The failure of the government to increase the benefits at a time when it has taken such a significant step in increasing so sharply the rate of contributions, represents one of the substantial deficiencies of this series of amendments which is now before us. The amendments do not basically affect the rate of benefits. I say they should be increased in the light of the value of Canadian currency at this time, the cost of living and all the ensuing obligations which are incurred by our people as a result of policies put forward by this government.
The minister made reference at one point to the report issued by the unemployment insurance advisory committee on August 18, 1958, which was tabled in accordance with the requirements of the Unemployment Insurance Act. In this connection it is worth observing the terms of the Unemployment Insurance Act itself. Section 89, subsection (1) reads:
(1) Within four months after the end of each fiscal year the advisory committee shall make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the fund as of the end of that fiscal year and shall also make a report to the governor in council on the financial condition of the fund whenever the advisory committee considers that the fund is or is likely to become, and is likely to continue to be, insufficient to discharge its liabilities, and may make a report on the financial condition of the fund at such other times as the advisory committee may think fit.
This advisory committee is an important body. On it sit four representatives of the employers. Their names are Mr. James Hunter, Norman Hesler, H. Shoobridge, and Mr. T. C. Urquhart. In addition there are four representatives of employees, Mr. George Burt, Mr. Stanley Knowles, who substitutes for someone else; Mr. Jean Marchand, and Mr. J. G. McLean. And the chairman of this advisory committee is the former deputy minister of labour, Mr. Arthur MacNamara. This report was tabled in accordance with the requirements of the statute, the pertinent section of which I have just referred to. The report itself is of great relevancy to the subject we have before us at this time. By the way, this report is addressed to the governor in council. Under the act I would submit that every report of the advisory committee must be addressed to the governor in council.


The unemployment insurance commission is a unique body. The commission was established so as to remove it from the ordinary routine of departmental administration and the reports it makes are made to the cabinet as a whole-to the governor in council-rather than to the minister in particular. The first section of the report reads:
Section 89(1) of the Unemployment Insurance Act requires the unemployment insurance advisory committee to report not later than July 31 each year on the financial condition of the unemployment insurance fund as at the preceding March 31.
That is clearly in accordance with the act. The reason for my emphasizing this section will be clear, I think, in the light of what I shall have to say about the supplementary report which the Minister of Labour in answer to requests by the opposition today tabled just prior to our adjournment at six o'clock.
In the third paragraph of this report the advisory committee points out:
The balance at the credit of the unemployment insurance fund at March 31, 1958, was $744,200,124.87, a decrease of $134,241,341.68 in the twelve-month period.
And then with some significance the committee goes on to point out:
This compares with an increase of $18,970,908.62 in the fiscal year 1956-57, an increase of $13,186,624.99 in the fiscal year 1955-56, and a decrease in the fiscal year 1954-55 of $41,245,135.50.
In paragraph 8 on page 2 of the report we find these words:
It should be mentioned that there was a revenue from investment of the fund of nearly $24 million. This item will be approximately $7 million less next year.
Of course, the reason for that was the unemployment insurance fund experienced the same difficulty that attended all the holders of government securities at that particular time. In paragraph 9 of the report the committee states:
The staggering increase in benefit payments is mainly due to the large number of unemployed workers during the period, and to the extension of the period during which seasonal benefits were available.
In paragraph 12 it is stated:
In the seventeen years, over $1] billion have been paid out in benefit payments.
On page 3 the report contains a table showing the balance at the credit of the unemployment insurance fund for the years 1955, 1956, 1957 and 1958. The balance in 1955 was $846,284,000 and in 1958 it was $744,200. I have already indicated that in 1959 it was $496.3 million. Paragraph 17 on page 4 states:
The committee calls attention to the serious drain on the fund created by the heavy load of payments during the year.

We come then to paragraph 19 which states:
There was, unquestionably, a need for the special provisions to meet the emergent situation last winter. The committee is gratified to find that the benefit payments could be made so satisfactorily through the commission offices.
Paragraph 20 is extremely significant:
It is a fact, however, that the burden of this expense, in the opinion of the committee, should not be imposed on the unemployment insurance fund unless the loss to the fund is made good.
That is the recommendation, the statement and the view of this advisory committee of employers and employees. In paragraph 21 they say:
We trust the government will take action to replace the drain on the fund, by reason of the extension of the seasonal benefit period by a grant.
This government has not accepted that recommendation made by this advisory committee which recommends that what was done on three previous occasions should be done by this administration so as not to place on the two main contributors a burden which in all fairness does not exclusively belong to them.
One could go on and look at various other sections of the report to find that the advisory committee by statistical analysis supports the contentions that it has made, that the fund should be supported by grants from the government and that the burden should not be shared only by the employers and employees. In paragraph 30 we find this statement:
You will observe Mr. Humphrys' estimate that an increase of 20 per cent in the contribution rates would probably maintain the fund at the present level. The estimate is based on the assumption that a pattern of employment during the next five years, may be expected, similar to that of the last five.
That is the view of this committee, repeating the observations of Mr. Humphrys that an increase of 20 per cent in the contribution rates would probably maintain the fund at the present level but that is not what is in this bill. This bill provides for increased rates of contributions to be imposed on the workers and on the employers in some categories of 30 per cent and in some other categories of slightly over 30 per cent. Can there be any doubt that the government for reasons that it has not explained has not pursued the practice of its predecessors in this particular and has failed to carry out the recommendations of the advisory committee set up for the purpose of advising the government and the commission in these matters?
I do not say it is the obligation of the government to accept the recommendations of bodies such as this one but surely it is an obligation of the government in the presentation of legislation such as this to explain
Unemployment Insurance Act why it has not carried out the recommendations of the advisory committee, recommendations that are made only after the most careful consideration.

As my hon. friend says, this is another hidden report. This report covers several meetings of the unemployment insurance committee convened on August 19,	1958. "Status of the fund";
attached to this report is a statement of revenues and expenditures for the period July 1, 1941 to July 31, 1958.
In the first paragraph, the report goes on to point out the situation is that during the past 16 months the balance in the fund has been reduced by $234,283,645.05. Here is an observation which undoubtedly the Minister of Labour, and understandably, was anxious that we should not carefully observe in connection with the matter now before the house. The report goes on to say;
The excess of payments, over revenue, persuades the committee it would be improper to recommend major changes at this time. That is changes which would very materially increase the deficit: or in the alternative would necessitate a tax on industry and workers.
The committee wishes to reserve its opinion on the "benefit formula proposal" of July 24, 1958 until the commission, and actuary, have had more opportunity to give it careful consideration in the light of further experience with the existing act.
In the meantime, we respectfully draw your attention to our report of July 18, 1958.
Incidentally, I would ask the minister if we could be provided with the benefit formula proposal which is referred to by the advisory committee to enable us to formulate a judgment as to whether or not the proposed rates, in the absence of increased benefits, are justified; so that we can compare our information with that before the advisory committee before we make up our minds on this important measure.
Then, the committee goes on to point out:
The committee recommends for your favourable consideration the following proposals of the unemployment insurance commission:
(1)	revise existing schedules of contribution and benefit rates by the addition of two new classes at the top of the earnings range.
The committee accepts that particular recommendation. Then, the second one is;
(2)	readjust and consolidate some of the lower classes:

That is not concurred in by this committee and is information which I believe is important in considering what we should do at the present time.
Then thirdly:
Revised rates of allowable earnings.
The committee accepts that. Then the committee goes on to point out on page 2:
The committee respectfully recommends that the division of responsibility for revenue to the fund as between employers, employees and government be adjusted so that the contribution from each be made equal. In other words, that the contribution from the government be made equal to one-half that of the combined contribution from employers and employees.
That recommendation is refused by the government and is in consequence not embodied in the legislation now before us. As the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) points out, the committee persist in this recommendation, having already made it in the earlier report which was tabled in accordance with section 89 of the act.
Then other recommendations were made which are not accepted by the government. For instance, it has not accepted the committee's endorsation of the proposal of the commission that the rule for determining dependancy rate be revised to avoid frequent changes in classification in respect to dependency. Then here is the significant thing. The Minister of Labour said that this report was made as a result of a request which he made to the advisory committee. Here is one of the concluding paragraphs:
A draft of the foregoing was read at the concluding session. Certain changes were suggested and made.
It was agreed that a proposed report, based on the draft, would be prepared and sent to members, to wire approval, or to suggest changes.
Messrs. Hunter, Hesler, Shoobrldge and Urquhart approve.
Messrs. Burt and Andras-
These were two of the labour representatives.
-sent an identical telegram which is quoted:
"Reur proposed report dated August 20 of unemployment insurance advisory committee regret do not find it possible to attach signature. Feel committee should be reconvened to review benefit formula proposal of July 24 possibly in October with view to modification or in light of further study by actuary. Feel also committee should withhold comments until minister has notified it of intentions regarding recommendations contained in our report dated July 18."
Mr. Marchand of the Catholic syndicates sent a wire to the same effect. Mr. McLean, the other labour representative, was absent and unable to attend the meeting.
Mr. Speaker, in the face of this report which the minister says he was not obliged to table in accordance with the requirements of the
Unemployment Insurance Act act we have here further evidence of the disagreement of the advisory committee with some of the policies embodied in this legislation which is now before the house. Either this advisory committee is a useful body and its recommendations are to be taken seriously, or we are to be told by the minister that such is not the case. At least we have the right to be told why these recommendations, originally in the report of August 18 unanimously concurred in, are not accepted by the government of the day.
We are called upon to impose a further contribution on employers and employees to the extent of 30 per cent. That is no ordinary imposition to impose upon the two segments of our population, and we in this house have the right to know why the government has failed to carry out the recommendation of the advisory committee. We have that right in the face of the circumstances that attend the presentation of the report for the first time in public as the result of a question put to the Minister of Labour this afternoon as to whether or not such a report was in existence. We do not even know whether the Minister of Labour has complied with the recommendation and the request of the advisory committee for further meetings. Was any meeting held in October? Was the advisory committee advised of this particular legislation? Were all of these proposed amendments placed before the advisory committee? Does this legislation, apart from the differences in the recommendations which it made, not now meet with the desire or point of view of this committee which was established to represent employers and labour and to advise the commission and the government? Surely we have the right to know what is the situation in that regard.
A difficulty may be because three members of that advisory committee representing labour have resigned from the commission. In this connection I call the minister's attention to section 19 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, which says:
(1)	There shall be a committee, called the ''unemployment insurance advisory committee", consisting of a chairman and not less than six nor more than eight other members, appointed by the governor in council to hold office during pleasure.
(2)	At least one of the members of the advisory committee, other than the chairman, shall be appointed after consultation with organizations representative of workers and an equal number after consultation with organizations representative of employers.
That is a requirement of the act. At the present time three members of that body are not functioning and may have resigned. Does the minister think that he is now complying with the act in carrying on the advisory

Unemployment Insurance Act committee when three labour members are not functioning? Subsection 1 of section 19 says:
There shall be a committee, . . . consisting of a chairman and not less than six nor more than eight other members, appointed by the governor in council-
At the present time there are only five functioning members of that committee other than the chairman. Does the minister think the act is being complied with at the present time? Is it permissible for him to bring in legislation of this kind and not have consulted a body set up, not by the government but by act of parliament for the purpose of advising the government on the very kind of measure now before us? It is a measure which adds rates of contribution to the extent of 30 per cent on the employers and workers. Does the minister think that he is complying with the statute in providing for that kind of a recommendation without having consulted the members of the advisory committee?
I say that this act passed by this parliament has been violated by the minister not only with regard to sections 89 and 90 but also with regard to the violation I have just referred to in section 19. This particular legislation, in order to carry with it the support it must have from the employers and the employees, should have been discussed at least in principle with this committee, a committee which has not sat since last August. We are told by this government which claims that it specially cherishes the rights of parliament, in effect and by implication, that we do not need this advisory committee. True, it has been set up by parliament, but the government knows what to do. It disregards this agency created by parliament because it has its own ideas of what should be embodied in this legislation. This from a government whose Prime Minister is about to bring in a bill of rights; this from a Prime Minister who has established himself in the minds of some people as the foremost champion of the rights of free people and the rights of a free parliament.
Let us examine the situation further and see whether there have been any other violations of this act. I asked the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) this afternoon if in the month of April the government had made any loans to the unemployment insurance commission. The Minister of Finance did not know. He was not certain whether or not in the month of April or in the month of May loans were made by the government of the day. I have before me, Mr. Speaker, a copy of order in council P.C. 1959/383, certified to be a true copy of a minute of a meeting

of the privy council approved by His Excellency the Governor General on April 2, 1959. This order in council is, of course, available to all hon. members as it was to me. The order states:
The committee of the Privy Council advise that Your Excellency may be pleased, pursuant to section 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act, to authorize the Minister of Finance to make loans from time to time to the unemployment insurance fund in an aggregate principal amount of $50 million.
Such a large amount, one would have thought, would have been in the mind of the Minister of Finance when a question was put to him a few weeks ago as to whether or not the government had made a loan to the unemployment insurance commission. But the minister did not remember, and I call the attention of the house to the significant date, April 2, 1959. That date is significant for reasons I will ultimately show. I pass over the first recommendation as not being immediately relevant, but here is recommendation No. 2:
That the said notes be signed by a commissioner and the secretary of the commission and bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent per annum.
This is an order in council dated April 2, 1959. And the rate specified is to be 5 per cent per annum. That percentage, Mr. Speaker, was imposed by a government which is opposed, so it says, to tight money. It was imposed by a government which promised to reduce interest rates after the very document which was tabled in the report of August 18 revealed that the unemployment insurance commission held fifth, sixth, seventh, eighth and ninth victory loan bonds which bore a rate of interest of 3 per cent. And this government, dedicated to the principle of easy money, nevertheless imposed upon the unemployment insurance commission a rate of 5 per cent. And then there is this most unusual arrangement set out in paragraph 3, namely:
That the loan be additionally secured by pledge of government of Canada direct and guaranteed bonds with a market value of at least 105 per cent of the loan.
In other words, the government's own body is saddled with a fixed rate. There is no market play here. What is open on the security market to the people of Canada generally holding bonds is denied for some reason by the Minister of Finance to the unemployment insurance commission with respect to the kind of yield that it might expect from the sale of its own securities. The Minister of Finance would lend this money, but the security must have a market value; not the market value which is current, but a market value of at least 105 per cent of the loan.

Again, here is a most unusual arrangement. Paragraph 4 states that the loan is to be repaid from the proceeds of the sale of government of Canada direct and guaranteed bonds at the sole discretion of the Minister of Finance, or from the cash resources of the fund. What authority is there for this kind of imposition "at the sole discretion of the Minister of Finance"? I say that the Minister of Finance must tell us what authority he has for exercising this kind of authority. There certainly is no statutory justification for his making that kind of condition with respect to such a loan.
But the most interesting part of this document, as I said at the outset, is the date. Under sections 84, 85 and 86 of the Unemployment Insurance Act the minister is given authority under certain conditions, which I do not propose to analyse now, to extend credit to the unemployment insurance commission. I hope that hon. members will peruse these sections carefully in order to ascertain whether in fact the minister acted in accordance with the act. But I call the attention of the house particularly to section 87:
The Minister of Finance shall report annually to parliament the state of the fund as of the 31st day of March last preceding and the transactions under section 86 during the fiscal year ending on that day; and the operations of the fund shall be set out in the public accounts in such detail as the Minister of Finance may decide.
Now the Minister of Finance did comply with this section of the act. He did report annually to parliament on the state of the fund as of the 31st day of March. But is it conceivable that on the thirtieth day of March, let us say, the Minister of Finance did not know of the intention on the part of the government to make a loan to the unemployment insurance commission in the amount of $50 million? Is it conceivable that the Minister of Finance or his advisers were not aware of the fact that there was about to be a transaction moving from the government through the Department of Finance to the unemployment insurance commission covering a loan of no less than $50 million? I suggest that the reason why this particular order in council is dated April 2, 1959 is because this government, with its large deficit this year and last year, and saddled by its promises to reduce these deficits while at the same time supplying additional benefits, would have been embarrassed by having to make once again in the report which it had to table on March 31 some reference to a further expenditure to the unemployment insurance commission in the amount of $50 million.
And what is amazing is that the actual transfer of funds took place on April 7. The order in council is dated April 2. There 66968-9-225
Unemployment Insurance Act is an actual transfer of funds from the Minister of Finance to the unemployment insurance commission on April 7, and on April 9 the Minister of Finance delivered his annual budget to the nation. In that budget he referred to the unemployment insurance fund. In a single paragraph he mentioned that the fund had suffered some diminution as a result of the invasions made on it. He made no reference whatsoever to the fact that only two days earlier he had transferred some $50 million to the commission. And, as he said today, that was not the kind of thing to which he had to refer in his annual financial statement to the nation. That is perhaps a clear indication that the Minister of Finance has not fully understood the obligations of a minister of finance. But if he did not mention it on April 9, can he find any excuse whatsoever in the light of the debate which ensued, for his not advising the house before the budget debate concluded that there had been a transfer of this large amount. The budget debate concluded on April 22, and from April 9 to April 22 it is inexplicable, in view of the repeated references which were made to the unemployment insurance fund, that the Minister of Finance should not have advised the house of this heavy borrowing by the fund.
As I said, the budget debate ended on April 22. And then the most amazing thing happened. On the next day we had another order in council providing for a further loan to the unemployment insurance commission. The budget debate had concluded on the 22nd and the minister was, then, safe from any likely interrogation as to whether or not moneys had been transferred from the Department of Finance to the unemployment insurance commission. It will not be forgotten that during the budget debate I asked the Minister of Finance whether or not the unemployment insurance commission had lost any money as a result of its forced participation in the bond conversion scheme of the government of Canada. The Minister of Finance said that that was not the kind of question obviously that could be replied to; that it was not in the public interest. One did not disclose the contents of the portfolios of those holding government securities, was his answer. I tried the question another way. I sent a written question to the Minister of Labour. Whether or not there was collaboration between the two, the information which was denied me by the Minister of Finance was supplied by the Minister of Labour when he told us that the unemployment insurance commission as a result of its forced participation in the bond conversion scheme of this government had lost over $10 million. That was the kind of information that could not be :. *: -s2
3552	HOUSE OF
Unemployment Insurance Act disclosed by the Minister of Finance so we had been told. I suppose the reason is now clear because, as I say, the next day, the 23rd, we had an order in council providing for an additional loan to the unemployment insurance commission of $30 million.
In the month of April we had two loans made by the government to the unemployment insurance commission in the amount of $80 million and the Minister of Finance today when asked whether or not such transfers had been made or whether any authority for loans of this character had been extended said he did not know. Is it conceivable that the Minister of Finance could not have known of these two transactions? He owes to the house an explanation as to why he did not include this information concerning the loans of $50 million and $30 million in the budget and why he did not reveal it to the house after the budget debate particularly when the Minister of Labour had revealed the extent of the loss as a result of bond conversion participation.
The terms of this order in council are interesting. The notes were to bear interest at the rate of 5 per cent per annum, the same condition as in the other order in council. The loans were to be additionally secured by pledge of the government of Canada direct and guaranteed bonds with a market value of at least 105 per cent of the loans. A further condition was that the loans be repaid from the proceeds of sale of government of Canada direct and guaranteed bonds at the sole discretion of the Minister of Finance or from the cash resources of the fund. This is a most unusual condition.
Why the Minister of Finance? What authority has he for giving himself this sole discretion? What statutory right exists for such an imposition? We have the right to ask the Minister of Finance and the Minister of Labour for an explanation of these particular loans. Why was not the unemployment insurance commission allowed to cash its own securities? If it had done that it would possibly have been able to make some money or, depending on the state of the market, it might have lost some money. In any event it had securities in its own possession. Its portfolio is a matter for the public to see. Why did the Minister of Finance And it necessary to make loans when the commission could easily have made its position liquid? I say it was only because the investment committee about which I am going to have a word to say was composed in such a manner as to make available to the commission only one course and that was a course that would not in any way have embarrassed the administration, by selling bonds below their face value.


What other explanation can there be unless, depending on the state of the market on that particular day, the commission could have sold the bonds at a profit? In any event I have no doubt that the reason for these transactions was that the government did not want to be embarrassed in any way and therefore the government was not going to allow the unemployment insurance commission to make transactions as normally it would in disposing of its securities in a manner that was conducive to its own interests.
It is interesting to note that section 20 of the Unemployment Insurance Act provides that investment transactions under sections 85, 86 and 87 shall be made only on the authorization of an investment committee of three members, one nominated by the Minister of Labour, one nominated by the Minister of Finance, and the governor of the Bank of Canada. It happens that those nominated include the deputy minister of finance and the deputy minister of labour. Does anyone think that this investment committee as presently constituted in the face of the present government's financial policy was free to allow the unemployment insurance commission to take the kind of action that would provide some liquidity from its securities?
I think the Minister of Finance owes the house an explanation of these various transactions. I ask him now some questions to which I think replies should be given before this debate concludes. What amounts were loaned by the Minister of Finance to the unemployment insurance fund during the months of April and May to the present date? Are these the only orders in council? Are these the only transactions made by the government to the commission? What issues of government bonds were pledged by the commission to secure these loans? At the time these loans were made was there outstanding to the credit of the unemployment insurance fund not sufficient for the payment of benefits under the act as required by paragraph 1 of section 86 of the act? Will the Minister of Finance report to the house on the amounts of various securities including treasury bills held by the unemployment insurance fund as of March 31, 1959? What were the purchases and sales of various obligations of or guaranteed by the government of Canada including treasury bills for each month of the last fiscal year and at what prices were these transactions made? What were the amounts of each victory loan issue held by the unemployment insurance fund sold during the conversion operation or converted into each conversion bond issue? Those are questions which in this matter we feel have great relevancy to the present situation.

Mr. Speaker, that is the very question with which I have been dealing. I said that the unemployment insurance commission has securities in the amount of many millions of dollars. If it required cash to meet benefit obligations all it had to do was liquidate those securities. Why was that liquidation not permitted? Was it because the government felt that the consequences would be embarrassing to it with regard to its particular financial policy? I do not know. I am simply asking the government to explain why it made these transactions. I am also asking the government to clearly establish that in the face of this situation it had the authority to extend this credit at a time when the unemployment insurance commission was in a position to meet its own obligations.
No one in this house questions the value of unemployment insurance. We sitting in the opposition under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Pearson) belong to a group that was responsible for presenting this legislation to the house in the dark days of the war. We were the first to introduce the principle of supplementary payments and we replenished the fund whenever we did provide for these supplementary payments. We support the principle of supplementary payments in the face of the serious unemployment problem that now confronts Canada; but we say that those payments given to people out of work to help to keep them alive should be borne by all of the taxpayers of the country and not imposed on the workers and on the employers of Canada exclusively.
We do not quarrel with the necessity of meeting the exigencies of this fund in the face of the perilous position in which we find it. We say that this perilous position could have been mitigated if the government had taken the right kind of steps to replenish the fund at the time they invaded it for the legitimate objective of providing supplementary benefits. We say that this bill is deficient because it imposes an abnormally high rate of contribution on the workers and on the employers of our country at a time when they are heavily taxed, without providing compensatory benefits certainly in proportion to the increased rates of contribution.
66968-9-225J
Unemployment Insurance Act
We say that this measure is only half right; we say that this measure does not give us the confidence which otherwise we would possess if we were satisfied that there had been the fullest consultation between the government and the advisory committee of the unemployment insurance commission. We say we would have greater confidence in this measure if we had been satisfied that some of the recommendations made by the advisory committee had been recognized by this government, if there had been an increase in the benefits to those who were called upon to pay the additional contributions. For these reasons I move, seconded by the hon. member for Laurier (Mr. Chevrier):
That all the words after "that" be struck out and the following substituted therefor:
"this house declines to proceed with a bill, the terms of which do not provide that the contribution from the government to the fund be made equal to one-half that of the existing combined contributions from employers and employees."
The terms of this amendment, Mr. Speaker, are in harmony with the recommendations unanimously made by the unemployment insurance advisory committee in the summer of 1958.

-the opposition ought to be placed at least in a position where they are able to consider the recommendations that the minister has received as to amendments to this act at the time at which we were supposed to receive them. In the amendments the minister is advocating added burdens upon the workers and employers of Canada. It is merely another case, as I indicated on another matter this afternoon, of again adding to the tax burden of the people of the country. I hope the minister and the government will realize that the way out of our difficulty is not by adding to the burdens of the working people of the country. The solution is an expansion of our economy and greater employment. When we have greater employment, more


people paying into the unemployment insurance fund and fewer people enjoying the benefits of the fund we will work our way out of the problem we are now seized with much more readily than if the only solution is to add to the burdens of those who are still usefully employed.
The minister is asking us to agree to a 30 per cent additional imposition on the workers and yet only 1 per cent of that additional burden is necessary to meet the extension of the benefits from 36 to 52 weeks. The average worker in Canada is being asked to pay 30 per cent more into the fund than he has been paying. However, if and when he becomes unemployed he will receive nothing by way of additional benefits with the exception that if he is unemployed for more than 36 weeks he will have the assurance that he can obtain benefits for 52 weeks.
Actually what the minister is asking the workers of Canada to do is to pay more money into the pool so that the government of Canada will not be faced with a completely denuded and depleted unemployment insurance fund within a very short time. Only 1 per cent of the 30 per cent is needed to pay for the extension from 36 weeks to 52 weeks of seasonal benefits. All the rest of the added impost on the workers of Canada is intended to replenish the fund. The minister should realize, and I gather he does, that the inadequacies of his own government are the cause of the economic recession. They are the cause of the unusually high level of unemployment and are responsible for the heavy burden being imposed on the unemployment insurance fund. Yet the minister is asking the workers of Canada to make up for the lack of adequate government policy.
Our group agrees that the seasonal benefits should be extended from 36 to 52 weeks. I should like to make the plea at this time that the act be amended in such a way that a gradually rising scale of benefits will be available. It is all right to ask an unemployed person to get by on $24 or $30 a week for a limited number of weeks. However, when his period of unemployment extends to months then the need for a higher weekly benefit is obvious. I believe that the act should be amended to provide for a graduated seal? so that if a person is unemployed for three, four, five or six months he will receive a higher weekly income than if he is unemployed only for a limited number of weeks.
I also believe that the act should be amended along the lines of the resolution placed on the order paper by the hon. member for Timmins (Mr. Martin) in which he advocates that enterprises which are vulnerable and may only continue in operation for

a limited period of time should pay an extraordinary amount into the fund so that if what is commonly called a ghost town develops, if a mine or other enterprise completely closes down, there will be some help available to the insured workers over and above their normal weekly unemployment insurance benefits.
I should also like to have seen in the amendments that the minister is now proposing the adoption of the philosophy that in the Unemployment Insurance Act we have the best machinery yet devised for looking after the welfare of our unemployed. I regret that under the act as it now stands the employable unemployed, after the expiry of a certain number of weeks, are advised that there is no more assistance available and that if they need help in order to maintain their homes and their families they must now apply to the social welfare office of their local municipal government. I believe that the Unemployment Insurance Act provides us with machinery that might adequately look after the welfare of all employable Canadians. I have advocated on a number of occasions that the act should be so amended so that when a man's regular benefits have expired he will continue to receive benefits from the unemployment insurance commission. I also advocate that the unemployment insurance commission should be recompensed for these benefits out of the consolidated revenue fund. The economy as a whole should absorb the expense.
The Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Churchill) is not here and has been absent on many other such occasions. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Fleming) is absent. They always leave the Minister of Labour to absorb the brunt of the attack. The Minister of Trade and Commerce ought to be here. He ought to show this house how, if we will now agree to the amendments proposed, his plan for the expansion of trade will relieve the problem a few months hence. The Minister of Finance ought to be here and ought to explain that, while this added taxation may be necessary at this moment, he has plans whereby there will be an economic expansion in the nation so that a year hence we might have hopes of reducing the impost on the working people of the country.
Our contention is that we should have in Canada an ever rising standard of living. It has never been our philosophy to pull anyone down. We do not believe that we build a better society that way, rather all our efforts ought to be directed toward bringing everyone up. We believe that an expanding economy and a policy of full employment would eliminate many of the difficulties with which the Minister of Labour is faced. We regret very much that the Minister of Labour
Unemployment Insurance Act has to be held responsible for the proposed amendments to the act. We do contend, however, that the Minister of Labour is offering nothing to the working people of Canada except an added imposition, an imposition that may be necessary because of the inadequacies of the government in supplying us with an expanding economy and full employment.

I rise on a point of order, Mr. Speaker. I doubt very much whether this amendment is a proper amendment. Your Honour will notice that it reads that this house decline to proceed with a bill, the terms of which do not provide-and so on. Now, surely that is covered by a ruling to be found on page 170 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, where he says:
An amendment proposing a direct negative, though it may be covered up by verbiage, is out of order.
This amendment is a straight negative that the house decline to proceed with a bill. How can you get an amendment that is more truly a direct negative than that? I refer Your Honour also to paragraph 14 on that same page of Beauchesne:
An amendment which would produce the same result as if the original motion were simply negatived is out of order.
Hon. members in the two opposition parties are free to vote against this bill, and they may produce quite a few reasons why they propose to vote against it, but surely they are not entitled to move amendments on the basis of those arguments that they use against the bill. However, this is exactly what this amendment seeks to do. Then, I refer Your Honour also to page 279 of Beauchesne's fourth edition, citation 389, the opening sentence of which reads as follows:
A motion opposing the second reading of a bill must not anticipate amendments which may be moved in committee. Alterations which may be affected by amending the clauses of the bill cannot be moved on the second reading.
We have only had a short time to check up the rules in regard to this amendment, but I do suggest that even on the citations which I have read the amendment is clearly out of order.

speechtext:
Tomorrow we shall continue with this debate; then take item No. 6 on today's order paper, the second reading of an act to amend the Federal-Provincial TaxSharing Arrangements Act; then the resolution which appears on government notices of motion today having to do with the Bretton Woods agreement; then item No. 15, a resolution concerning the convention covering the abolition of forced labour; then, item No. 13, a resolution preceding a measure on the Defence Services Pension Act; item No. 2, second reading of an act to confirm an agreement between the government of Canada and the government of New Brunswick respecting Indian reservations; item No. 11, a resolution approving the convention on the nationality of married women.
After that, we will take the estimates of the Department of Labour, and then the estimates of the Department of Public Works. There may have to be some change for Wednesday, but in any event we start with that tomorrow, at least.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Is it the intention to proceed with this work in that order during the course of the whole week?

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: I cannot say about the order on Wednesday, but tomorrow we will proceed in this order. There is a chance that if the report of the special committee considering the Canadian National Railways and the Trans-Canada Air Lines is tabled we may go on with the resolution which appears today under government notices of motion concerning the expenditures of the C.N.R.

Mr. Speaker, may I say on that point that that is a very involved item of legislation, and if the printed records of the committee are not available until tomorrow I do not think the house leader would want us to go into the capital expenditures of the C.N.R. as rapidly as was suggested.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: We would meet the wishes of the members opposite with regard to that.

speakerposition: stagedirection
speechtext: At ten o'clock the house adjourned, without question put, pursuant to standing order.﻿MAY 11. 1959
